title: From the shop floor
intro: Shopping tips, storage advice and seasonal buying notes from the people who stock the shelves.

items.title: How to do a month's grocery shop without overspending
items.author: Store team
items.excerpt: Buying for a month costs less per kilo but needs a plan. Here's the order we recommend shopping in, and where bulk stops paying.

body.text: Buying monthly nearly always beats buying weekly on price — but only if what you buy actually gets used. The waste is where the saving disappears.
Start with what does not spoil
Rice, atta, dal, oil and sugar keep for months in a sealed container. Buy those in the largest pack your storage allows, because the per-kilo price drops sharply above 5 kg.
Then work backwards through the fridge
Milk, curd and greens are the opposite: buy them weekly, or you throw money away. Our monthly lists split the two groups for exactly this reason.
Where bulk stops paying
Spices lose their aroma after about six months. Cooking oil goes rancid. Biscuits go soft. For those, the mid-size pack is the honest answer, whatever the shelf label says.

items.title: Storing vegetables so they last twice as long
items.author: Store team
items.excerpt: Most vegetables are thrown away because of how they were stored, not how old they were. Six changes that make the difference.

body.text: The single biggest cause of waste in a home kitchen is putting everything in the same drawer.
Keep onions and potatoes apart
Onions give off moisture and gas that sprouts potatoes early. Store them in separate baskets, both somewhere dark and airy — never in the fridge.
Greens want a damp cloth, not a bag
Wrap spinach and coriander in a lightly damp cotton cloth before refrigerating. A sealed plastic bag traps condensation and rots them from the leaf tips inward.
Tomatoes are not a fridge item
Below about 12°C the texture goes mealy and the flavour flattens. Keep them on the counter, stem side down.

items.title: Reading a food label properly takes ten seconds
items.author: Store team
items.excerpt: Ignore the front of the pack. Three things on the back tell you almost everything worth knowing.

body.text: The front of a packet is marketing. The back is regulated. Only one of them is worth your time.
Ingredients are listed by weight
Whatever comes first is what there is most of. If sugar is in the first three on a breakfast product, it is a dessert.
Check per 100 g, not per serving
Serving sizes are chosen by the manufacturer and are often unrealistically small. The per-100 g column is the only way to compare two brands fairly.
"No added sugar" is not "no sugar"
Fruit juice concentrate is still sugar. The nutrition table settles the question in a way the claim on the front never does.

items.title: Why we tell people to do festival shopping three weeks early
items.author: Store team
items.excerpt: Prices on dry fruits, oil and ghee climb steadily in the fortnight before any major festival. Here's how to get ahead of it.

body.text: It is not that shops raise prices out of greed. Wholesale rates genuinely climb as demand concentrates into two weeks, and we pay those rates too.
Buy the keepers early
Dry fruits, ghee, oil and sugar all store well. Buying them three weeks out routinely saves 15–20% against festival-week prices.
Leave the perishables late
Flowers, sweets and fresh produce should be bought as close to the day as possible, regardless of price. Buying those early costs you more in waste than you save.

items.title: Lunchbox ideas that survive until lunchtime
items.author: Store team
items.excerpt: A packed lunch has to still be good four hours later. That rules more out than most parents expect.

body.text: The test is not whether it tastes good at 7 am. It is whether it tastes good at 1 pm, unrefrigerated, after being carried in a bag.
What holds up
Parathas, idlis, lemon rice, besan chilla and anything with a dry rather than wet masala. These are still pleasant at room temperature.
What does not
Anything with fresh curd stirred through, cut apple, or a thin gravy. They separate, brown, or leak.

items.title: You only need four things in the cleaning cupboard
items.author: Store team
items.excerpt: Most households own nine cleaning products and use three. Here's the short list that actually covers a home.

body.text: Specialist cleaners are mostly the same surfactants at different dilutions, sold in different bottles.
The four
A dishwash gel, a floor disinfectant, a laundry detergent and a general surface spray will handle everything in a normal home. Add a scouring powder if you cook a lot.
Buy concentrate where you can
Floor cleaner in particular is sold ready-diluted at a large markup. The concentrate costs less per wash and takes up a quarter of the shelf.
